summary: Merge all overlapping intervals into a minimal set of disjoint intervals.
mainInsight: After sorting by start, overlapping intervals are adjacent: an interval overlaps the last merged one iff its start <= that interval's end, in which case extend the end with max(end, end'); otherwise start a new interval.

approaches.name: Sort by start + linear sweep
approaches.summary: Maintain the last merged interval and extend or append.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal. Note the aliasing with the input's inner lists.

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Sort by start, then sweep: extend the last merged interval when the next start is at most its end. Clue: Intervals can overlap in any input order, but after sorting by start every overlap involves the neighbouring interval, so one sweep merges them.
keyPoints: Intervals can overlap in any input order, but after sorting by start every overlap involves the neighbouring interval, so one sweep merges them.
cards.explanation: Sorting by start puts every interval that could overlap the current one right after it, so a single pass extends or closes the running interval.

promptVariants: What is the first step of Merge Intervals and why?
cards.explanation: After sorting by start, an interval can only overlap the most recent merged interval.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Sort by end time: Possible for other problems (e.g. non-overlapping intervals) but not the standard merge approach.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Use a heap of ends: Used for meeting-room style counting, not merging.

promptVariants: Why is it enough to compare each interval only with the last merged one?
cards.answer: Sorted by start, if an interval does not overlap the last merged interval then it starts after that interval's end and therefore after every earlier interval's end, so it cannot overlap any earlier one. Two intervals overlap iff the later one's start <= the earlier one's end.
keyPoints: Only the last merged interval can overlap
cards.explanation: The merged end is max(end, new end).
Sort O(n log n), sweep O(n).

promptVariants: What is the extra space and what does `ans.append(intervals[i])` imply about aliasing?
cards.answer: O(n) for the output (plus sort space). Appending the input's inner list and then mutating ans[-1][1] also mutates the caller's interval object; copy the interval (e.g. list(intervals[i])) if the input must stay unchanged.
keyPoints: Shares inner lists with the input
cards.explanation: The in-place sort also reorders the input list.

promptVariants: Why is the condition `ans[-1][1] < intervals[i][0]` (strict) the 'no overlap' test, and what about touching intervals like [1,4],[4,5]?
cards.answer: A new interval is separate only if it starts strictly after the previous end; touching intervals ([1,4] and [4,5]) share the point 4 and are merged by the problem's definition. The merged end must be the maximum because the new interval may be fully contained in the previous one (e.g. [1,10] and [2,3]).

cards.explanation: [2,3] and [3,7] share the endpoint 3, so they merge into [2,7]; [9,10] is separate.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[[2,3],[3,7],[9,10]]: Touching intervals count as overlapping, so they merge.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[[2,7]]: [9,10] does not touch [2,7], so it stays separate.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[[2,3],[9,10]]: No interval may be dropped; every value must stay covered.
